blocks.text: It is proved that שפן saphan is not the rabbit, as they claim, but a kind of larger mouse in Eretz Yisrael, Egypt and Libya, which is called Δίπους [Dipous] by Herodotus and others, Χοιρογρύλλιος [Choirogryllios] by the Elders, Ἀρκτομῦς [Arktomys] by Jerome, and اليربوع [al-yarbūʿ] aljarbuo by the Arabs; about it many things not yet published are brought forward from the writings of the Arabs.

In Levit, XI, 5. and Deut. XIV, 7., among the animals which do chew the cud but [col. 1002] do not have a cloven hoof, and are therefore unclean, השפן, ὁ σαφάν [ho saphan], is listed together with the camel and the hare. The plural שפנים sephanim occurs in Psal. CIV. 18.: The rock is a refuge לשפנים, τοῖς σεφανίμ [tois sephanim]. And in Prov. XXX, 26.: שפנים sephanim, a feeble folk, make their home in the rock. Most of the more recent interpreters explain them as rabbits. Many things seem on the face of it to favour this interpretation. 1. That twice in the law השפן is joined with הארנבת, that is, with the hare, as a kindred animal. 2. That the passage of the Psalm just cited is rendered thus in the Greek edition: Πέτρα καταφυγὴ τοῖς λαγωοῖς [Petra kataphygē tois lagōois], The rock is a refuge for hares. Some copies have τοῖς χοιρογρυλλίοις [tois choirogrylliois], that is, as they claim, for hedgehogs. But the most ancient writers follow the former reading. Jerome, Epistle 135 to Sunia and Fretela: All rendered χοιρογρυλλίους [choirogryllious] by a similar word; only the LXX translated hares. So too read Theodoret in his Commentary on this Psalm, Basil on Isaiah, chapter 2, and Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Πέτροις ἠλιβάτοις περιθάρσεες εἰσὶ λαγωοὶ, [Petrois ēlibatois peritharsees eisi lagōoi]

Trusting in sheer rocks are the hares: and the Arabic version, which was made from the Greek: The rock is a refuge الارانب [al-arānib] of hares. Others join both: thus Augustine on this passage: The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs and hares. Arnobius: There is the rock, offering refuge either to the young of hedgehogs, etc. or to hares. Bede on Proverbs, chapter 30: And it must be noted that in the Psalm, where we sing “The rock is a refuge for hedgehogs,” there is found in some codices “for hares,” in some “for choerogryllii.” 3. The Hebrew of Prov. XXX, 26., שפנים עם לא עצום, the Vulgate translator rendered thus: The little hare, a feeble folk, following, if I am not mistaken, [II, 410] some Greek interpreter who had explained שפנים as λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, that is, rabbits. For so in Strabo, book 3, λαγίδεις [lagideis], little hares, are taken for rabbits. The Greeks have no other name for the rabbit. For κόνιλος [konilos] in Aelian and κούνικλος [kouniklos] in Polybius and Galen were words proper to the Spaniards, and λεβηρὶς [lebēris] in Strabo and Erotian a word proper to the Massilians; they were not used in Greece. 4. The old Book of Names, which is ascribed to Philo, has this on Jeremiah: SAPHAN, choerogryllius, hare, or hedgehog. And on Ezekiel: SAPHAN, hedgehog, or hare. 5. In Giggeius's Arabic Lexicon, p. 854, vol. 2, سفن [safan] saphan is rendered cuniculus [rabbit]. Where he got this from, however, I do not know at all, for I have found it nowhere else. 6. The Hebrew name שפן saphan seems to allude to the Hebrew verbs ספן and צפן, of which the former means to cover, the latter to hide. And this seems to fit the rabbit, which seeks the hiding places of burrows in order to lurk in them and be, as it were, covered over. Martial:
The rabbit delights in dwelling in dug-out caves.
